extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary critics, and advanced creative-writing practitioners interested in narrative voice and focalization
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical framework for identifying and evaluating narrating instance, focalization (internal/external/double), modal signals, and temporal position of narrating in fiction; emphasizes how these choices shape what a narrative can legitimately report. Useful for close reading, theoretical analysis, or informed narrative craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modalizing locutions as indicators of focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of modalizing words/phrases (perhaps, undoubtedly, as if, seem, appear) allows the narrator to assert hypothetically what he could not affirm within internal focalization and functions as an 'alibi of the novelist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such locutions as markers of narrator stance and focalization; note that when multiple contradictory hypotheses are offered (e.g., three 'perhaps'es giving three explanations) their value as concealed authorial intrusions (paralepsis) is weakened while their function as indicators of focalization is strengthened. Examine frequency and multiplicity to decide whether the hesitation belongs to hero, narrator, or novelist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous internal focalization of perceptual descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions tied to a character's perception should not exceed what the perceiver actually sees/hears, and their duration should not exceed the real time of contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating focalized description, check that content and temporal length correspond to the hero's perceptual capacity; examples in Proust show scenes where only part of an event is perceived (e.g., hearing murmur from behind shutters), and the narrative scrupulously respects these perceptual limits. Avoid attribution of unseen details to a focalized consciousness unless there is an explicit narrating device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paralipsis as hyper-restriction (withholding within focalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paralipsis is the deliberate hyper-restriction of the field—omitting parts of events or whole episodes—consistent with internal focalization, often revealed later by the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize paralipses when the text withholds information that is only disclosed later by the narrator; consider whether the withholding is justified by narratoral perspective (autobiographical narrator) rather than by novelist omniscience. Use examples (end of passion, deaths, withheld episodes) to assess legitimacy and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolepsis and advance notices as narrator-level information
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses (advance notices) and locutions like 'I have learned since...' belong to the narrator's later knowledge and therefore exceed the hero's immediate capacities for knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute proleptic comments to the narrating instance (not the hero) in autobiographical narratives; they are legitimate insofar as they represent the narrator's handling of information. Evaluate opportuneness and tonal fit, but do not automatically equate such interventions with the omniscient novelist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative attribution: prefer narrator over omniscient novelist
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological rule: attribute to the omniscient 'novelist' only what cannot plausibly be ascribed to the (autobiographical) narrator; many seemingly omniscient details may be explained as narrator's later knowledge or hearsay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing narrative knowledge, attempt plausible diegetic sources (reports, gossip, the narrator's later discoveries) before positing novelist omniscience. Only mark an intervention as omniscient when no narratorial explanation is tenable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducible paralepsis indicating omniscience
rubrics_metrics.description: When the narrative reports another character's private thoughts or final thoughts at the moment they occur, with no plausible diegetic relay, this paralepsis is irreducible and must be ascribed to the novelist's omniscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag instances (e.g., last thoughts reported where no one could have known) as transgressions of autobiographical focalization; they evidence a third narrative mood (zero-focalization) and may intentionally disrupt the narrative system. Treat these as deliberate technical choices rather than errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual coherence and narrative tonality as decisive criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary criterion for judging narratorial interventions is not material possibility or psychological plausibility but textual coherence and narrative tonality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate narrative intrusions, prolepses, or omniscient passages on whether they cohere with the work's established tonality and internal logic. Even materially impossible knowledge can be legitimate if tonally coherent; conversely, plausible interventions can be illegitimate if they break tonal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polymodality: coexistence of multiple focalization modes
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative may simultaneously or alternately adopt focalization through the hero, the autobiographical narrator, and the omniscient novelist—resulting in a polymodal (polymodal/ polymodal) system rather than a single coherent code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and describe the coexistence and interaction of different focal modes (subjective hero, narrator, omniscient). Treat polymodality as an intentional, emblematic technique (e.g., Proust) that can subvert realist 'point of view' laws; analyze how shifts contribute to aesthetic effects (mimesis vs. narrative presence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double (concurrent) focalization and antithesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent or double focalization occurs when the narrative presents actions on one plane (hero-witness) and feelings on another (omniscient revelation), producing an antithesis organizing a passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for passages where subjective perception and what is 'revealed' about others' inner states run in parallel; analyze the antithetical effects (e.g., brutal actions vs. delicate feelings) and how the tension destabilizes realist illusion and creates literary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating instance autonomy: distinguish narrator from author and writing situation
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrating instance (enunciating subject) is a distinct fictional or discursive agent and should not be conflated with the real author or the act of writing; narrating situation can differ from writing circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating voice and reliability, treat the narrator as a constructed instance with spatio-temporal and interpersonal determinations (who speaks, when, to whom). Avoid automatically reading authorial intent into narrator statements; instead infer narratee, occasion, and enunciating constraints from textual traces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifts and permanences of narrating instance within a work
rubrics_metrics.description: A single narrative can change narrating instances (different 'I's or narrators) or maintain the same one throughout; such shifts are analytically significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map instances of narrator-change or embedding (embedded narrators, changes in narrating person) and assess their diegetic role and impact on focalization, reliability, and the unity of narration (e.g., Ulysses' Books IX–XII, multi-degree embeddings in Thousand and One Nights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal position of narrating relative to story (four types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate four narrating temporal positions: subsequent (past-tense, classical), prior/predictive (narrating precedes story), simultaneous (present-tense contemporaneous), and interpolated (narrating inserted between moments of the action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which temporal position(s) a text uses; each has characteristic effects (e.g., distance and retrospection in subsequent; prophetic tone in prior; immediacy in simultaneous; entanglement and plot-performativity in interpolated/epistolary forms). Use this to analyze narrator perspective and temporal friction between story and narrating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary/journal/interpolated narrating and the live/prerecorded friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms that mix 'live' (simultaneous) and 'prerecorded' (retrospective) narration (journals, letters, epistolary novels) produce a subtle friction between immediate report and later appraisal, often creating dissonance between 'hero-of-the-event' and 'narrator-of-the-event.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing voice, note how near temporal intervals produce counterpoints: the narrator's present stance can reframe past events, creating multiple temporal selves (e.g., Cecile of yesterday vs. Cecile of today). Examine performative plot effects (letters discovered, letters as plot devices) and the blending of interior monologue with after-the-event commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifying improbable observational situations within focalization code
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative scenes that strain plausibility (peeking through small windows, overhearing from a distance) are to be read as diegetic devices that confirm rather than violate the code of internal focalization—they dramatize the hero's difficulty in penetrating another's existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than dismissing unlikely observational set-ups as flaws, evaluate whether they function as legitimate internal focalization devices that limit perception and thus shape narrative knowledge; attribute such 'acrobatic indiscretions' to the demands of focal restriction and narrative economy.
